[Er48] Erdős, P., On arithmetical properties of Lambert series. J. Indian Math. Soc. (N.S.) (1948), 63-66.

Erdos363.IsInterval.docHtml: A finite set of naturals is an interval of naturals.

Erdos363.IsValidCollection.docHtml: A collection of intervals as in Erdős Problem 363.

Erdos363.erdos_363.docHtml:
Is it true that there are only finitely many collections of disjoint intervals $I_1,\ldots,I_n$ of size $\lvert I_i\rvert \geq 4$ for $1\leq i\leq n$ such that$$\prod_{1\leq i\leq n}\prod_{m\in I_i}m$$is a square?

This is false: Ulas [Ul05] constructed infinitely many such collections.

Erdos138.monoAP_guarantee_set.docHtml:
The set of natural numbers that guarantee a monochromatic arithmetic progression.

A number N belongs to this set if, for a given number of colors r and an arithmetic progression length k, any r-coloring of the integers {1, ..., N} must contain a monochromatic arithmetic progression of length k.

Erdos138.monoAP_guarantee_set_nonempty.docHtml: Asserts that for any number of colors r and any progression length k, there always exists some number N large enough to guarantee a monochromatic arithmetic progression. In other words, the set monoAP_guarantee_set is non-empty. This is the fundamental existence result that allows for the definition of the van der Waerden numbers.

Erdos138.monoAPNumber.docHtml: The van der Waerden number, is the smallest integer N such that any r-coloring of {1, ..., N} is guaranteed to contain a monochromatic arithmetic progression of length k. It is defined as the infimum of the (non-empty) set of all such numbers N.

Erdos138.W.docHtml: An abbreviation for the van der Waerden number for 2 colors, commonly written as W(k). This represents the smallest integer N such that any 2-coloring of {1, ..., N} must contain a monochromatic arithmetic progression of length k.

Erdos138.erdos_138.variants.prime.docHtml: When $p$ is prime Berlekamp [Be68] has proved $W(p+1) ≥ p^{2^p}$.

Erdos138.erdos_138.variants.difference.docHtml:
In [Er81] Erdős asks whether $W(k+1) - W(k) \to \infty$.

The DeepMind prover agent has found a formal proof of this statement.

Erdos213.Erdos213For.docHtml: The predicate (on $n$) that there exist $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, no three on a line and no four on a circle, such that all pairwise distances are integers.

Erdos213.erdos_213.docHtml: Let $n \geq 4$. Are there $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, no three on a line and no four on a circle, such that all pairwise distances are integers?

Erdos213.erdos_213.variants.KK08.docHtml: The best construction to date, due to Kreisel and Kurz, has $n = 7$.

Erdos141.Set.IsPrimeProgressionOfLength.docHtml: The predicate that a set s consists of l consecutive primes (possibly infinite). This predicate does not assert a specific value for the first term.

Erdos141.first_three_odd_primes.docHtml: The first three odd primes are an example of three consecutive primes.

Erdos141.Set.IsAPAndPrimeProgressionOfLe.docHtml: The predicate that a set s is both an arithmetic progression of length l and a progression of l consecutive primes.

Erdos141.exists_three_consecutive_primes.docHtml: There are 3 consecutive primes in arithmetic progression.

Erdos141.erdos_141.docHtml: Let $k≥3$. Are there $k$ consecutive primes in arithmetic progression?

Erdos141.erdos_141.variants.first_cases.docHtml: The existence of such progressions has been verified for $k≤10$.

Erdos141.erdos_141.variants.eleven.docHtml: Are there $11$ consecutive primes in arithmetic progression?

Erdos141.consecutivePrimeArithmeticProgr.docHtml: The set of arithmetic progressions of consecutive primes of length $k$.

Erdos141.erdos_141.variants.infinite_thr.docHtml: It is open, even for $k=3$, whether there are infinitely many such progressions.

Erdos141.erdos_141.variants.infinite_gen.docHtml: Fix a $k \geq 3$. Is it true that there are infinitely many arithmetic prime progressions of length $k$?

Erdos943.erdos_943.docHtml: Let $A$ be the set of powerful numbers. Is is true that $1_A\ast 1_A(n)=n^{o(1)}$ for every $n$?

Erdos98.h.docHtml: $h(n)$ is the minimum number of distinct distances determined by any $n$-point set in $\mathbb{R}^2$ in general position (no three collinear, no four cocyclic).

Erdos98.erdos_98.docHtml: Let $h(n)$ be such that any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, with no three on a line and no four on a circle, determine at least $h(n)$ distinct distances. Does $h(n)/n\to \infty$?

Erdos98.erdos_98.variants.upper_bound.docHtml: Erdős could not even prove $h(n)\geq n$. Pach has shown $h(n) < n^{\log_2 3}$. Erdős, Füredi, and Pach [EFPR93] have improved this to $h(n) < n\exp(c\sqrt{\log n})$ for some constant $c>0$.

Erdos266.erdos_266.docHtml:
Let $a_n$ be an infinite sequence of positive integers such that $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ converges. There exists some integer $t \ge 1$ such that $\sum \frac{1}{a_n + t}$ is irrational.

This was disproven by Kovač and Tao in [KoTa24].

[KoTa24] Kovač, V. and Tao T., On several irrationality problems for Ahmes series. arXiv:2406.17593 (2024).

Erdos266.erdos_266.variants.all_rational.docHtml:
In fact, Kovač and Tao proved in [KoTa24] that there exists a strictly increasing sequence $a_n$ of positive integers such that $\sum \frac{1}{a_n + t}$ converges to a rational number for all $t \in \mathbb{Q}$ such that $t \ne -a_n$ for any $n$.

[KoTa24] Kovač, V. and Tao T., On several irrationality problems for Ahmes series. arXiv:2406.17593 (2024).

Erdos946.erdos_946.docHtml: There are infinitely many $n$ such that $τ(n) = τ(n+1)$. Proved in [He84]. Here τ is the divisor counting function, which is σ 0 in mathlib.

Erdos946.erdos_946.variants.spiro_5040.docHtml: There are infinitely many $n$ such that $τ(n) = τ(n + 5040)$. Proved in [Sp81].

Erdos946.erdos_946.variants.heathbrown_l.docHtml: The number of $n \le x$ with $τ(n) = τ(n+1)$ is at least $x / (\log x)^7$ for all sufficiently large $x$. Proved in [He84].

Erdos914.erdos_914.docHtml:
Let $r\geq 2$ and $m\geq 1$. Every graph with $rm$ vertices and minimum degree at least $m(r-1)$ contains $m$ vertex disjoint copies of $K_r$.

When $r=2$ this follows from Dirac's theorem. Corrádi and Hajnal [CoHa63] proved this when $r=3$. Hajnal and Szemerédi [HaSz70] proved this for all $r\geq 4$.

A shorter proof was given by Kierstead and Kostochka [KiKo08].

Erdos914.erdos_914.variants.equitable_co.docHtml: Equivalently, every graph with $rm$ vertices and maximum degree at most $m-1$ has a proper vertex colouring with $m$ colours in which every colour class has exactly $r$ vertices (an equitable colouring).

Erdos516.OfFiniteOrder.docHtml: An entire function f is said to be of finite order if there exist numbers c, a ≥ 0 such that for all z, ‖f z‖ ≤ c * rexp (‖z‖ ^ a).

Erdos516.erdos_516.docHtml: Let f = ∑ aₖzⁿₖ be an entire function of finite order such that nₖ / k → ∞. Then limsup (fun r => ratio r f) atTop = 1. This is proved in [Fu63].

Erdos516.erdos_516.variants.limsup_ratio.docHtml: Let f = ∑ aₖzⁿₖ be an entire function such that nₖ > k (log k) ^ (2 + c). Then limsup (fun r => ratio r f) atTop = 1. This is proved in [Ko65].
Is it true that for all entire functions f = ∑ aₖzⁿₖ such that ∑' 1 / nₖ < ∞, limsup (fun r => ratio r f) atTop = 1?

Erdos624.ExistsEventuallySurjective.docHtml: The condition that an integer m ensures the existence of a function f covering Fin n for all large enough subsets Y. The property is invariant under bijection, so we use a representative Fin n for a finite set of size n.

Erdos624.H.docHtml: Let $H(n)$ be the minimum integer $m$ such that there is a function $f: \mathcal{P}(X) \to X$ where $X$ is a finite set of size $n$, such that for every subset $Y \subseteq X$ with $|Y| \ge m$, the set ${f(A) : A \subseteq Y}$ covers $X$.

Erdos624.erdos_624.docHtml: Let $X$ be a finite set of size $n$ and $H(n)$ be such that there is a function $f:{A : A\subseteq X}\to X$ so that for every $Y\subseteq X$ with $\lvert Y\rvert \geq H(n)$ we have $\left{ f(A) : A\subseteq Y\right}=X$. Prove that $H(n)-\log_2 n \to \infty$.

Erdos442.Set.bddProdUpper.docHtml: If A be a set of natural numbers and let x be real, then A.bddProdUpper x is the finite upper-triangular set of pairs of elements of A that are ≤ x. Specifically, it is the set {(n, m) | n ∈ A, n ≤ x, m ∈ A, m ≤ x, n < m}

Erdos442.erdos_442.docHtml:
Let $\operatorname{Log} x := \max{\log x, 1}$, $\operatorname{Log}2x = \operatorname{Log} (\operatorname{Log} x)$, and $\operatorname{Log}3x = \operatorname{Log}(\operatorname{Log}(\operatorname{Log} x)).$ Is it true that if $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ is such that $$ \frac{1}{\operatorname{Log}2 x} \sum{n\in A: n\leq x} \frac{1}{n}\to\infty $$ then $$ \left(\sum{n\in A: n\leq x} \frac{1}{n}\right)^2 \sum{n, m \in A: n < m \leq x} \frac{1}{\operatorname{lcm}(n, m)}\to\infty $$ as $x\to\infty$?

Tao [Ta24b] has shown this is false.

[Ta24b] Tao, T., Dense sets of natural numbers with unusually large least common multiples. arXiv:2407.04226 (2024).

Note: the informal and formal statements follow the solution paper https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.04226

Erdos442.erdos_442.variants.tao.docHtml:
Tao resolved erdos_442 in the negative in Theorem 1 of https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.04226. The following is a formalisation of that theorem with $C_0 = 1$.

Let $\operatorname{Log} x := \max{\log x, 1}$, $\operatorname{Log}_2x = \operatorname{Log} (\operatorname{Log} x)$, and $\operatorname{Log}3x = \operatorname{Log}(\operatorname{Log}(\operatorname{Log} x)).$ There exists a set $A$ of natural numbers such that $$ \sum{n\in A: n\leq x} \frac{1}{n} = \exp\left(\left(\left(\frac{1}{2} + o(1)\right)\operatorname{Log}2^{1/2}x \operatorname{Log}3x\right)\right) $$ and $$ \sum{n, m\in A: n, m\leq x} \frac{1}{\operatorname{lcm}(n, m)}\ll\left(\sum{n\in A: n\leq x} \frac{1}{n}\right)^2 $$

Erdos100.DistancesSeparated.docHtml: If two distances in A differ, they differ by at least 1.

Erdos100.erdos_100.docHtml: Is the diameter of $A$ at least $Cn$ for some constant $C > 0$?

Erdos100.erdos_100.variants.strong.docHtml: Stronger conjecture: diameter $\geq n - 1$ for sufficiently large $n$.

Erdos100.erdos_100.variants.kanold.docHtml: From [Kanold]: diameter $\geq n^{3/4}$. TODO: find reference

Erdos100.erdos_100_piepmeyer.docHtml: From [Piepmeyer]: 9 points with diameter $< 5$. TODO: find reference

Erdos789.IsSubsetSumSeparatingCard.docHtml: Given a non-negative integer $n$, we say $m$ is a separating cardinality of subset sums if, for any set $A$ of $n$ integers, there is some $B\subseteq A$ of size $\geq m$ such that subset sums of $B$ can only ever coincide when the subsets have the same cardinality.

Erdos789.subsetSumThreshold.docHtml: The subset sum threshold $h(n)$, for each positive $n$, is the maximal separating cardinality of subset sums for $n$.

Erdos789.erdos_789.docHtml:
Let $h(n)$ be maximal such that if $A\subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ with $\lvert A\rvert=n$ then there is $B\subseteq A$ with $\lvert B\rvert \geq h(n)$ such that if $a_1+\cdots+a_r=b_1+\cdots+b_s$ with $a_i,b_i\in B$ then $r=s$.

Estimate $h(n)$.

Erdos789.erdos_789.variants.sq.docHtml:
Let $h(n)$ be maximal such that if $A\subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ with $\lvert A\rvert=n$ then there is $B\subseteq A$ with $\lvert B\rvert \geq h(n)$ such that if $a_1+\cdots+a_r=b_1+\cdots+b_s$ with $a_i,b_i\in B$ then $r=s$.

Is $h(n) = \Theta(\sqrt{n})$?

Erdos789.erdos_789.variants.sq_isBigO.docHtml: By the solved variant erdos_789.variants.isBigO_sq, in order to prove erdos_789.variants.sq it suffices to show $\sqrt{n}=O(h(n))$.

Erdos789.erdos_789.variants.cube_root_li.docHtml:
Let $h(n)$ be maximal such that if $A\subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ with $\lvert A\rvert=n$ then there is $B\subseteq A$ with $\lvert B\rvert \geq h(n)$ such that if $a_1+\cdots+a_r=b_1+\cdots+b_s$ with $a_i,b_i\in B$ then $r=s$.

Is $h(n) = \Theta((n\log(n)))^{1/3})$?
Erdős [Er62c] and Choi [Ch74b] proved that $(n\log(n))^{1/3}\ll h(n)$.

Erdos789.erdos_789.variants.isBigO_cube_.docHtml: By the solved variant erdos_789.variants.cube_root_linearithmic_isBigO, in order to prove erdos_789.variants.cube_root_linarithmic it suffices to show $h(n) = O((n\log(n))^{1/3})$.

Erdos849.erdos_849.docHtml: Is it true that, for every integer $t\geq1$, there is some integer $a$ such that ${n \choose k} = a$ with $1\leq k \le \frac{n}{2}$ has exactly $t$ solutions?

Erdos307.erdos_307.docHtml:
Are there two finite set of primes $P$ and $Q$ such that

$$ 1 = \left( \sum_{p \in P} \frac{1}{p} \right) \left( \sum_{q \in Q} \frac{1}{q} \right) $$ ?

Asked by Barbeau [Ba76].

[Ba76] Barbeau, E. J., Computer challenge corner: Problem 477: A brute force program.

Erdos307.erdos_307.variants.coprime.docHtml:
Instead of asking for sets of primes, ask only that all elements in the sets be relatively coprime.

Cambie has found several examples when this weakened version is true. For example, $$ 1=\left(1+\frac{1}{5}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}\right) $$ and $$ 1=\left(1+\frac{1}{41}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{7}\right). $$

Erdos307.erdos_307.variants.coprime_one_.docHtml: There are no examples known of the weakened coprime version if we insist that $1\not\in P\cup Q$.

Erdos307.erdos_307.barrier.docHtml: A machine-checked barrier for Erdős 307 (Bonfioli, 2026): any solution with Q nonempty uses at least 59 primes in total, and (∏_{p ∈ P} p)² ≥ 4·10¹¹² — i.e. ∏_{p ∈ P} p ≥ 2·10⁵⁶ (and, by symmetry, the same for ∏ Q); so no solution lies below a prime-product of 2.09·10⁵⁶. The full sorry-free proof is in the linked repository (Closed.lean at tag v1.0.0): the left conjunct is card_ge_59, the right is erdos307_barrier_closed. The only non-logical input is a native_decide evaluation of the first 59 primes; the axioms are propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound together with that native_decide.

Erdos886.Erdos886Divisors.docHtml: The set of divisors of $n$ in the interval $(n^{1/2}, n^{1/2} + n^{1/2-\epsilon})$.

Erdos886.erdos_886.docHtml:
Let $\epsilon>0$. Is it true that, for all large $n$, the number of divisors of $n$ in $(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+n^{1/2-\epsilon})$ is $O_\epsilon(1)$?

Erdős attributes this conjecture to Ruzsa.

Erdos886.erdos_886.variants.rosenfeld_in.docHtml: Erdős and Rosenfeld [ErRo97] proved that there are infinitely many $n$ such that there are four divisors of $n$ in $(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+16n^{1/4})$.

Erdos886.erdos_886.variants.rosenfeld_bo.docHtml: Erdős and Rosenfeld [ErRo97] proved that, for any constant $C>0$, all large $n$ have at most $1+C^2$ many divisors in $[n^{1/2}, n^{1/2}+Cn^{1/4}]$.

Erdos996.fourierPartial.docHtml:
Erdős Problem 996

Reference:

    erdosproblems.com/996

    [Er49d] Erdös, P. "On the strong law of large numbers." Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 67.1 (1949): 51-56.

    [Ma66] Matsuyama, Noboru. "On the strong law of large numbers." Tohoku Mathematical Journal, Second Series 18.3 (1966): 259-269.

Erdos996.erdos_996.docHtml: Does there exists a positive constant C such that for all f ∈ L²[0,1] and all lacunary sequences n, if ‖f - fₖ‖₂ = O(1 / log log log k ^ C), then for almost every x, lim ∑ k ∈ Finset.range N, f (n k • x)) / N = ∫ t, f t ∂t?

Erdos996.erdos_996.variants.log2.docHtml: The following theorem is proved in [Ma66].

Erdos997.IsWellDistributed.docHtml:
Call $x_1,x_2,\ldots \in (0,1)$ well-distributed if, for every $\epsilon>0$, if $k$ is sufficiently large then, for all $n>0$ and intervals $I\subseteq [0,1]$, $\lvert # { n < m\leq n+k : x_m\in I} - \lvert I\rvert k\rvert < \epsilon k.$

The notion of a well-distributed sequence was introduced by Hlawka and Petersen [Hl55].

Erdos997.erdos_997.docHtml:
Is it true that, for every $\alpha$, the sequence ${ \alpha p_n}$ is not well-distributed, if $p_n$ is the sequence of primes?

The answer is yes, by [APSSV26, Section 4]; a Lean formalisation is available in [Mo26].

Erdos997.erdos_997.variants.lacunary.docHtml: Erdős proved that, if $n_k$ is a lacunary sequence, then the sequence ${ \alpha n_k}$ is not well-distributed for almost all $\alpha$.

Erdos997.erdos_997.variants.irrational.docHtml:
He also claimed in [Er64b] to have proved that there exists an irrational $\alpha$ for which ${\alpha p_n}$ is not well-distributed. He later retracted this claim in [Er85e], saying "The theorem is no doubt correct and perhaps will not be difficult to prove but I never was able to reconstruct my 'proof' which perhaps never existed."

The existence of such an $\alpha$ was established by Champagne, Le, Liu, and Wooley [CLLW24].

Erdos392.erdos_392.docHtml: Let $A(n)$ denote the least value of $t$ such that $$ n! = a_1 \cdots a_t $$ with $a_1 \leq \cdots \leq a_t\leq n^2$. Then $$ A(n) = \frac{n}{2} - \frac{n}{2\log n} + o\left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right). $$

Erdos392.erdos_392.variants.lower.docHtml: If we change the condition to $a_t \leq n$ it can be shown that $$ A(n) = n - \frac{n}{\log n} + o\left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right) $$

Erdos392.erdos_392.variants.implication.docHtml: Cambie has observed that a positive answer follows from the result above with $a_t \leq n$, simply by pairing variables together, e.g. taking $a'i = a{2i-1}a_{2i}$ (and the lower bound follows from Stirling's approximation).

Erdos884.sumDivisorInvPairwiseDifference.docHtml: The sum $\sum_{1 \le i < j \le \tau(n)} \frac{1}{d_j - d_i}$ over all pairs of divisors $d_i < d_j$ of $n$.

Erdos884.sumDivisorInvConsecutiveDiffere.docHtml: The sum $\sum_{1 \le i < \tau(n)} \frac{1}{d_{i + 1} - d_i}$ over consecutive divisors of $n$.

Erdos884.Erdos884Prop.docHtml:
For a natural number n, let $1 = d_1 < \dotsc < d_{\tau(n)} = n$ denote the divisors of $n$ in increasing order. Does it hold that $\sum_{1 \le i < j \le \tau(n)} \frac{1}{d_j - d_i} \ll 1 + \sum_{1 \le i < \tau(n)} \frac{1}{d_{i + 1} - d_i}$ for $n \to \infty`, i.e. $\sum_{1 \le i < j \le \tau(n)} \frac{1}{d_j - d_i} \in O \left( 1 + \sum_{1 \le i < \tau(n)} \frac{1}{d_{i + 1} - d_i}) \right)$?

This conjecture has been disproved:

    In September 2025, Terence Tao gave a conditional negative answer assuming the prime tuples conjecture, see erdos_884_false_of_hardy_littlewood for this implication.

    Daniel Larsen subsequently gave an unconditional disproof.

Erdos884.erdos_884.docHtml:
For a natural number n, let $1 = d_1 < \dotsc < d_{\tau(n)} = n$ denote the divisors of $n$ in increasing order. Does it hold that $\sum_{1 \le i < j \le \tau(n)} \frac{1}{d_j - d_i} \ll 1 + \sum_{1 \le i < \tau(n)} \frac{1}{d_{i + 1} - d_i}$ for $n \to \infty`, i.e. $\sum_{1 \le i < j \le \tau(n)} \frac{1}{d_j - d_i} \in O \left( 1 + \sum_{1 \le i < \tau(n)} \frac{1}{d_{i + 1} - d_i}) \right)$?

This conjecture has been disproved:

    In September 2025, Terence Tao gave a conditional negative answer assuming the prime tuples conjecture, see erdos_884_false_of_hardy_littlewood for this implication.

    Daniel Larsen subsequently gave an unconditional disproof.

Reference: erdosproblems.com/884

Erdos884.erdos_884_false_of_hardy_little.docHtml: In September 2025, Terence Tao gave a conditional negative answer to Erdos conjecture 884, disproving it under the assumption of the Qualitative Hardy-Littlewood Conjecture. See here. The qualitative version of the conjecture only states that there are infinitely many tuples of primes and does not require any asymptotical bounds and as such is a corollary of the general form of the Hardy-Littlewood Conjecture. We state the 'weaker' implication using general Hardy-Littlewood here, since this conjecture is already formalized.

Erdos229.erdos_229.docHtml:
Let $(S_n)_{n \ge 1}$ be a sequence of sets of complex numbers, none of which have a finite limit point. Does there exist an entire transcendental function $f(z)$ such that, for all $n \ge 1$, there exists some $k_n \ge 0$ such that $f^{(k_n)}(z) = 0$ for all $z \in S_n$.

This is Problem 2.30 in [Ha74], where it is attributed to Erdős.

Solved in the affirmative by Barth and Schneider [BaSc72].

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.

Erdos229.theorem_1.docHtml: Let ${S_k}$ be any sequence of sets in the complex plane, each of which has no finite limit point. Then there exists a sequence ${n_k}$ of positive integers and a transcendental entire function $f(z)$ such that $f^{(n_k)}(z) = 0$ if $z \in S_k$.

Erdos1023.F.docHtml: F n is the maximal size of a family of subsets of ${1,\ldots,n}$ such that no set in this family is the union of other members of the family.

Erdos1023.erdos_1023.docHtml:
Let $F(n)$ be the maximal size of a family of subsets of ${1,\ldots,n}$ such that no set in this family is the union of other members of the family. Is it true that there is a constant $c>0$ such that $$F(n)\sim c \frac{2^n}{n^{1/2}}?$$

Hunter observes in the comments that this follows from the solution to [447], which implies $F(n)\sim \binom{n}{n/2}$.

Erdos1023.erdos_1023.variants.erdos_klei.docHtml: Erdős and Kleitman proved in unpublished work that $$F(n)\asymp \frac{2^n}{n^{1/2}}.$$ ([Er71] has an exponent of $3/2$, but this is presumably a typo.)

Erdos1023.erdos_1023.variants.hunter.docHtml: Hunter observes in the comments that this follows from the solution to [447], which implies $F(n)\sim \binom{n}{n/2}$.

Erdos647.erdos_647.docHtml: Let $\tau(n)$ count the number of divisors of $n$. Is there some $n > 24$ such that $$ \max_{m < n}(m + \tau(m)) \leq n + 2? $$

Erdos647.erdos_647.variants.lim.docHtml: Erdős says 'it is extremely doubtful' that there are infinitely many such $n$, and in fact suggests that $$ lim_{n\to\infty} \max_{m < n}(\tau(m) + m − n) = \infty. $$

Erdos647.erdos_647.variants.infinite.docHtml: Erdős says it 'seems certain' that for every $k$ there are infinitely many $n$ for which $$ \max_{n−k < m < n}(m + \tau(m)) ≤ n + 2. $$

Erdos967.summand.docHtml: The summand $\frac{1}{n^{1+it}}$, for a natural number $n$ and $t\in\mathbb{R}$.

Erdos967.erdos_967.docHtml:
Let $1<a_1<\cdots$ be a sequence of integers such that $\sum\frac{1}{a_i}<\infty$. Is it true that, for every $t\in \mathbb{R}$, $$1+\sum_{k}\frac{1}{a_k^{1+it}}\neq 0?$$

Yip [Yi25] has proved that this is not always true - in fact, for any real $t\neq 0$, there exists a sequence of integers $1<a_1<\cdots$ such that $\sum \frac{1}{a_i}<\infty$ and $1+\sum_{k}\frac{1}{a_k^{1+it}}=0$.

This was formalized in Lean by Wu using Aristotle.

Erdos967.erdos_967.variants.yip.docHtml: Yip [Yi25] has proved that this is not always true - in fact, for any real $t\neq 0$, there exists a sequence of integers $1<a_1<\cdots$ such that $\sum \frac{1}{a_i}<\infty$ and $1+\sum_{k}\frac{1}{a_k^{1+it}}=0$.

Erdos967.erdos_967.variants.finite.docHtml: It remains open whether this is true for every finite sequence of integers.

Erdos967.erdos_967.variants.two_three_fi.docHtml: A question of Erdős and Ingham [ErIn64]. The simplest case they could not decide this question for was the finite sequence ${2,3,5}$.

Erdos967.erdos_967.variants.tauberian.docHtml: Their interest in this problem arose from their proof that the statement that there are no such zeros is equivalent to the fact that, for any non-decreasing $f:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ which is bounded on every bounded interval and is $=0$ for $x<1$, the relationship $$f(x)+\sum_k f(x/a_k)=\left(1+\sum_k \frac{1}{a_k}+o(1)\right)x$$ implies $f(x)=(1+o(1))x$.

Erdos798.gridPoints.docHtml: The grid ${1,\ldots,n}^2$, viewed as a set of points of the plane.

Erdos798.IsLineCover.docHtml: S is a set of points of ${1,\ldots,n}^2$ such that the lines determined by the pairs of distinct points of S cover all points of ${1,\ldots,n}^2$.

Erdos798.t.docHtml: The minimum number of points in ${1,\ldots,n}^2$ such that the lines determined by these points cover all points in ${1,\ldots,n}^2$.

Erdos798.erdos_798.docHtml:
Let $t(n)$ be the minimum number of points in ${1,\ldots,n}^2$ such that the $\binom{t}{2}$ lines determined by these points cover all points in ${1,\ldots,n}^2$.

Estimate $t(n)$. In particular, is it true that $t(n)=o(n)$?

A problem of Erdős and Purdy, who proved $t(n) \gg n^{2/3}$.

Resolved by Alon [Al91] who proved $t(n) \ll n^{2/3}\log n$.

Erdos798.erdos_798.variants.lower_bound.docHtml: A problem of Erdős and Purdy, who proved $t(n) \gg n^{2/3}$.

Erdos798.erdos_798.variants.upper_bound.docHtml: Resolved by Alon [Al91] who proved $t(n) \ll n^{2/3}\log n$.

Erdos1056.AllModProdEqualsOne.docHtml: The proposition that the modular product of a collection of consecutive interval equals $1$ modulo $p$, where intervals are defined by a function specifying the consecutive boundaries.

Erdos1056.erdos_1056.docHtml: Let $k ≥ 2$. Does there exist a prime $p$ and consecutive intervals $I_0,\dots,I_k$ such that $\prod\limits_{n{\in}I_i}n \equiv 1 \mod n$ for all $1 \le i \le k$?

Erdos1056.erdos_1056.variants.k2.docHtml: This is problem A15 in Guy's collection [Gu04], where he reports that in a letter in 1979 Erdős observed that $3 * 4 \equiv 5 * 6 * 7 \equiv 1 \mod 11$.

Erdos1056.erdos_1056.variants.noll_simmo.docHtml: Noll and Simmons asked, more generally, whether there are solutions to $q_1! \equiv \dots \equiv q_k! \mod p$ for arbitrarily large $k$ (with $q_1 < \dots < q_k$).

Erdos96.convexUnitDistanceCounts.docHtml: The set of all possible numbers of unit distances determined by the vertices of a convex $n$-gon.

Erdos96.convexUnitDistanceCounts_bddAbov.docHtml: This lemma confirms that the set of possible unit-distance counts is bounded above, which ensures that taking the supremum (sSup) is a well-defined operation. The trivial upper bound is the total number of pairs of points, $\binom{n}{2}$.

Erdos96.maxConvexUnitDistances.docHtml: The maximum number of unit distances determined by the vertices of a convex $n$-gon. This function is often denoted as $U_c(n)$ in combinatorics.

Erdos96.erdos_96.docHtml: If $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ form a convex polygon then there are $O(n)$ many pairs which are distance $1$ apart.

Erdos398.erdos_398.docHtml: Brocard's Problem Does $n! + 1 = m^2$ have integer solutions other than $n = 4, 5, 7$?

Erdos355.erdos_355.docHtml:
Is there a lacunary sequence $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ (so that $A={a_1 < \cdots}$ and there exists some $\lambda > 1$ such that $a_{n+1}/a_n\geq \lambda$ for all $n\geq 1$) such that $$\left{ \sum_{a\in A'}\frac{1}{a} : A'\subseteq A\textrm{ finite}\right}$$ contain all rationals in some open interval?

Bleicher and Erdős conjectured the answer is no.

In fact the answer is yes, with any lacunarity constant $\lambda\in (1,2)$ (though not $\lambda=2$), as proved by van Doorn and Kova\v{c} [DoKo25].

This was formalized in Lean by van Doorn using Aristotle.

Erdos401.erdos_401.docHtml:
Is there some function $f(r)$ such that $f(r)\to \infty$ as $r\to\infty$, such that, for infinitely many $n$, there exist $a_1,a_2$ with $$a_1+a_2> n+f(r)\log n$$ such that $a_1!a_2! \mid n!2^n3^n\cdots p_r^n$?

It is ambiguous in [ErGr80] what the intended quantifiers are on the variables (they write 'is it true that we can find $a_1+a_2>n+f(r)\log n$...'). Comparing to previous problems such as [728] and [729] it seems most likely that they intended to ask the formulation in the problem statement.

The answer is yes: Barreto and Leeham have used ChatGPT to provide a proof of the stated problem (in fact essentially the same construction as their solution to [729]).

Erdos306.erdos_306.docHtml: Let $\frac a b\in \mathbb{Q}_{>0}$ with $b$ squarefree. Are there integers $1 < n_1 < \dots < n_k$, each the product of two distinct primes, such that $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{1}{n_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{n_k}$?

Erdos306.erdos_306.variants.integer_thre.docHtml: Every positive integer can be expressed as an Egyptian fraction where each denominator is the product of three distinct primes.

Erdos352.erdos_352.docHtml: Is there some $c > 0$ such that every measurable $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ of measure $\geq c$ contains the vertices of a triangle of area 1?

Erdos359.IsGoodFor.docHtml: The predicate that A is monotone, A 0 = n and for all j, A (j + 1) is the smallest natural number that cannot be written as a sum of consecutive terms of A 0, ..., A j

Erdos359.erdos_359.parts.i.docHtml: Let $a_1< a_2 < ⋯ $ be an infinite sequence of integers such that $a_1=1$ and $a_{i+1}$ is the least integer which is not a sum of consecutive earlier $a_j$s. Show that $a_k / k \to \infty$.

Erdos359.erdos_359.parts.ii.docHtml: Let $a_1< a_2 < ⋯ $ be an infinite sequence of integers such that $a_1=1$ and $a_{i+1}$ is the least integer which is not a sum of consecutive earlier $a_j$s. Show that $a_k / k ^ {1 + c} \to 0$ for any $c > 0$.

Erdos359.erdos_359.variants.isGoodFor_1_.docHtml: Suppose monotone sequence $A$ satisfies the following: A 0 = 1 and for all j, A (j + 1) is the smallest natural number that cannot be written as a sum of consecutive terms of A 0, ..., A j. Then the first few terms of $A$ are $1,2,4,5,8,10,14,15,...$.

Suppose monotone sequence $A$ satisfies the following: A 0 = 1 and for all j, A (j + 1) is the smallest natural number that cannot be written as a sum of consecutive terms of A 0, ..., A j. Then it is conjectured that $$a_k ~ \frac{k \log k}{\log \log k}$$.

Erdos1059.erdos_1059.docHtml: Are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p - k!$ is composite for each $k$ such that $1 ≤ k! < p$?

Erdos325.IsSumThreePower.docHtml: A predicate for $n$ to be the sum of three $k$th powers.

Erdos325.cardIsSumThreePowerBelow.docHtml: The number of integers $\leq x$ which are the sum of three $k$th powers.

Erdos325.erdos_325.docHtml: Writing $f_{k, 3}(x)$ for the number of integers $\leq x$ which are the sum of three $k$th powers, is it true that $f_{k, 3}(x) \gg x ^ (3 / k)$?

Erdos325.erdos_325.variants.weaker.docHtml: Writing $f_{k, 3}(x)$ for the number of integers $\leq x$ which are the sum of three $k$th powers, is it even true that $f_{k, 3}(x) \gg_{\epsilon} x ^ (3 / k - \epsilon)$?

Erdos325.erdos_325.variants.wooley.docHtml: For $k = 3$, the best known is due to Wooley [Wo15] [Wo15] Wooley, Trevor D., Sums of three cubes, II. Acta Arith. (2015), 73-100.

Erdos1072.f.docHtml: For any prime $p$, let $f(p)$ be the least integer such that $f(p)! + 1 \equiv 0 \mod p$.

Erdos1072.erdos_1072.parts.i.docHtml: Is it true that there are infinitely many $p$ for which $f(p) = p − 1$?

Erdos1072.erdos_1072.parts.ii.docHtml: Is it true that $f(p)/p \to 0$ for $p \to \infty$ in a density 1 subset of the primes?

Erdos1072.erdos_1072.variants.littleo.docHtml:
Erdős, Hardy, and Subbarao [HaSu02], believed that the number of $p \le x$ for which $f(p)=p−1$ is $o(x/\log x)$.

[HaSu02] Hardy, G. E. and Subbarao, M. V., A modified problem of Pillai and some related questions. Amer. Math. Monthly (2002), 554--559.

Erdos694.erdos_694.docHtml:
Let $f_\max(n)$ be the largest $m$ such that $\phi(m) = n$, and $f_\min(n)$ be the smallest such $m$, where $\phi$ is Euler's totient function. Investigate $$ \max_{n\leq x}\frac{f_\max(n)}{f_\min(n)}. $$

GPT-5.5 Pro (prompted by Price) has proved (see also the comments for a summary) that $$ \max_{n\leq x}\frac{f_{\max}(n)}{f_{\min}(n)}=(e^\gamma+o(1))\log\log x. $$

A Lean formalisation of the reduction exists, conditional on Mertens' product theorem and Linnik's theorem; see the formal proof.

Erdos694.erdos_694.variants.carmichael.docHtml: Carmichael has asked whether there is an integer $n$ for which $\phi(m) = n$ has exactly one solution, that is $\frac{f_\max(n)}{f_\min(n)} = 1$.

Erdos694.erdos_694.variants.inf_unique.docHtml: Erdős has proved that if there exists an integer $n$ for which $\phi(m) = n$ has exactly one solution, then there must be infinitely many such $n$.

Erdos351.imageSet.docHtml:
The set of rational numbers of the form P(n) + 1 / n where n is a natural number and P is a polynomial with rational coefficients.

Note: We include P 0 in there (since 1 / 0 = 0), but this doesn't change the validity of the conjecture

Erdos351.IsStronglyComplete.docHtml: The predicate that a set A is strongly complete, i.e. that for every finite set B, every sufficiently large integer is a sum of elements of the set A \ B.

Erdos351.HasCompleteImage.docHtml: The predicate that the rational polynomial P has a complete image.

Erdos351.erdos_351.docHtml: Let $p(x) \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ be a non-constant rational polynomial with positive leading coefficient. Is it true that $$A={ p(n)+1/n : n \in \mathbb{N}}$$ is strongly complete, in the sense that, for any finite set $B$, $$\left{\sum_{a \in X} a : X \subseteq A \setminus B, X \textrm{ is finite}\right}$$ contains all sufficiently large integers?

Erdos351.erdos_351.variants.X.docHtml: Let $p(x) = x \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$. It has been shown that $$A={ p(n)+1/n : n \in \mathbb{N}}$$ is strongly complete, in the sense that, for any finite set $B$, $$\left{\sum_{a \in X} a : X \subseteq A \setminus B, X \textrm{ is finite}\right}$$ contains all sufficiently large integers.

Erdos351.erdos_351.variants.X_sq.docHtml: Let $p(x) = x ^ 2 \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$. It has been shown that $$A={ p(n)+1/n : n \in \mathbb{N}}$$ is strongly complete, in the sense that, for any finite set $B$, $$\left{\sum_{a \in X} a : X \subseteq A \setminus B, X \textrm{ is finite}\right}$$ contains all sufficiently large integers.

Erdos212.erdos_212.docHtml: Is there a dense subset of ℝ^2 such that all pairwise distances are rational?

Erdos224.erdos_224.docHtml:
If $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is any set of $2^d+1$ points then some three points in $A$ determine an obtuse angle.

The general case was proved by Danzer and Gr"{u}nbaum [DaGr62].

Erdos517.erdos_517.docHtml: If f(z) = ∑ aₖzⁿₖ is an entire function (with aₖ ≠ 0 for all k) such that nₖ / k → ∞, is it true that f assumes every value infinitely often?

Erdos517.erdos_517.variants.fejer.docHtml: If f(z) = ∑ aₖzⁿₖ is an entire function (with aₖ ≠ 0 for all k) such that ∑ 1 / nₖ < ∞, then f assumes every value infinitely often. This theorem is proved in [Bi28].

Erdos848.NonSquarefreeProductProp.docHtml: A set $A$ has the non-squarefree product property if $ab + 1$ is not squarefree for all $a, b ∈ A$.

Erdos848.A₇.docHtml: The candidate extremal set: ${n ∈ {0, \dots, N-1} : n ≡ 7 (mod 25)}$.

Erdos848.Erdos848For.docHtml: The Erdős Problem 848 statement for a fixed $N$: any set $A ⊆ {0, \dots, N-1}$ with the non-squarefree product property has cardinality at most $|A₇(N)|$.

Erdos848.erdos_848.docHtml:
Is the maximum size of a set $A ⊆ {1, \dots, N}$ such that $ab + 1$ is never squarefree (for all $a, b ∈ A$) achieved by taking those $n ≡ 7 \pmod{25}$?

This asks whether Erdos848 N holds for all $N$ (formulated using A ⊆ Finset.range N).

This was solved for all sufficiently large $N$ by Sawhney in this note. In fact, Sawhney proves something slightly stronger, that there exists some constant $c>0$ such that if $\lvert A\rvert \geq (\frac{1}{25}-c)N$ and $N$ is large then $A$ is contained in either ${ n\equiv 7\pmod{25}}$ or ${n\equiv 18\pmod{25}}$.

Erdos848.erdos_848.variants.asymptotic.docHtml:
There exists $N₀$ such that for all $N ≥ N₀$, if $A ⊆ {1, \dots, N}$ satisfies that $ab + 1$ is never squarefree for all $a, b ∈ A$, then $|A| ≤ |{n ≤ N : n ≡ 7 \pmod{25}}|$.

More precisely, Sawhney proves: there exist absolute constants $η > 0$ and $N₀$ such that for all $N ≥ N₀$, if $|A| ≥ (1/25 - η)N$ then $A ⊆ {n : n ≡ 7 \pmod{25}}$ or $A ⊆ {n : n ≡ 18 \pmod{25}}$.

A complete formal Lean 4 proof is available at: https://github.com/The-Obstacle-Is-The-Way/erdos-banger

Erdos4.erdos_4.docHtml: Is it true that, for any $C > 0$, there infinitely many $n$ such that: $$ p_{n + 1} - p_n > C \frac{\log\log n\log\log\log\log n}{(\log\log\log n) ^ 2}\log n $$

Erdos4.erdos_4.variants.rankin.docHtml: Rankin's theorem: there exists a positive constant $C$ such that Erdos4For C holds.

Erdos698.erdos_698.docHtml:
Is there some $h(n)\to \infty$ such that for all $2\leq i<j\leq n/2$ $$\textrm{gcd}\left( \binom{n}{i},\binom{n}{j}\right) \geq h(n)?$$

This was resolved by Bergman [Be11], who proved that for any $2\leq i<j\leq n/2$ $$\textrm{gcd}\left( \binom{n}{i},\binom{n}{j}\right) \gg n^{1/2}\frac{2^i}{i^{3/2}},$$ where the implied constant is absolute.

Erdos698.erdos_698.variants.erdos_szeker.docHtml: A problem of Erdős and Szekeres, who observed that $$\textrm{gcd}\left( \binom{n}{i},\binom{n}{j}\right) \geq \frac{\binom{n}{i}}{\binom{j}{i}} \geq 2^i$$ (in particular the greatest common divisor is always $>1$).
This inequality is sharp for $i=1$, $j=p$, and $n=2p$.

Erdos698.erdos_698.variants.bergman.docHtml: This was resolved by Bergman [Be11], who proved that for any $2\leq i<j\leq n/2$ $$\textrm{gcd}\left( \binom{n}{i},\binom{n}{j}\right) \gg n^{1/2}\frac{2^i}{i^{3/2}},$$ where the implied constant is absolute.

Erdos502.erdos_502.docHtml:
What is the size of the largest $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ such that there are only two distinct distances between elements of $A$? That is, $$# { \lvert x-y\rvert : x\neq y\in A} = 2.$$

Asked to Erdős by Coxeter. Bannai, Bannai, and Stanton [BBS83] have proved that $$\lvert A\rvert \leq \binom{n+2}{2}.$$ A simple proof of this upper bound was given by Petrov and Pohoata [PePo21].

The exact maximum is not known in general: a lower bound of $\binom{n+1}{2}$ follows from the construction of Alweiss (see [503]).

Erdos45.erdos_45.docHtml:
Let $k\geq 2$. Is there an integer $n_k$ such that, if $D={ 1<d<n_k : d\mid n_k}$, then for any $k$-colouring of $D$ there is a monochromatic subset $D'\subseteq D$ such that $\sum_{d\in D'}\frac{1}{d}=1$?

This follows from the colouring result of Croot [Cr03]. Croot's result allows for $n_k \leq e^{C^k}$ for some constant $C>1$ (simply taking $n_k$ to be the lowest common multiple of some interval $[1,C^k]$). Sawhney has observed that there is also a doubly exponential lower bound, and hence this bound is essentially sharp.

Erdos330.Rep.docHtml:
Rep A m h means m is a sum of exactly h elements of A, which is m ∈ h • A.

Exactly h rather than at most h, for two reasons. It is the notion Erdős states the problem with, via f_2(m), the number of solutions of m = a_i + a_j [Er80]. And it is the notion IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder uses below, so the statement is not switching between two meanings of "representable" partway through.

Allowing fewer than h summands also breaks the statement outright: taking one summand makes every element of A count as represented, so UnrepWithout A n h would contain no element of A besides possibly n. Those are exactly the integers the problem is about. If a ∈ A with a ≠ n is only expressible as a = n + b, it cannot be represented without n and belongs in the set, but the one-element sum a itself would have excluded it.

Erdos330.UnrepWithout.docHtml: Integers not representable as a sum of exactly h elements of A while avoiding n.

Erdos330.MinAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder.docHtml: An asymptotic additive basis of order h is minimal when one cannot obtain an asymptotic additive basis by removing any element from it.

Erdos330.erdos_330_statement.docHtml:
Does there exist a minimal basis $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ with positive density such that, for any $n \in A$, the (upper) density of integers which cannot be represented without using $n$ is positive?

Neither set is asked to have a density, only to have positive upper density, so Set.upperDensity is used for both rather than Set.HasPosDensity. As with many of Erdős' questions "positive density" here most likely means positive upper density, and in [Er80] he considers either the lower or the upper density for the integers not representable without a fixed n. Requiring the density to exist would ask a strictly harder question than the one posed. See #3979.

Such a set exists, so the answer is yes. The linked proof gives one of order 2.

Erdos409.erdos_409.parts.i.docHtml: How many iterations of $n\mapsto\phi(n) + 1$ are needed before a prime is reached?

Erdos409.erdos_409.variants.termination.docHtml: If $n > 0$, then the iteration $n\mapsto\phi(n) + 1$ necessarily reaches a prime.

Erdos409.erdos_409.parts.i.isTheta.docHtml: Let $c(n)$ be the minimum number of iterations of $n\mapsto\phi(n) + 1$ before a prime is reached. What is $\Theta(c(n))$?

Erdos409.erdos_409.parts.i.isBigO.docHtml: Let $c(n)$ be the minimum number of iterations of $n\mapsto\phi(n) + 1$ before a prime is reached. Find the simplest function $g(n)$ such that $c(n) = O(g(n))$?

Erdos409.erdos_409.parts.i.isLittleO.docHtml: Let $c(n)$ be the minimum number of iterations of $n\mapsto\phi(n) + 1$ before a prime is reached. Find the simplest function $g(n)$ such that $c(n) = o(g(n))$?

Erdos409.erdos_409.parts.ii.docHtml: Can infinitely many $n$ reach the same prime under the iteration $n\mapsto\phi(n) + 1$?

Erdos409.erdos_409.parts.iii.docHtml: What is the density of $n$ which reach any fixed prime under the iteration $n\mapsto\phi(n) + 1$?

Erdos409.erdos_409.variants.sigma.docHtml: How many iterations of $n\mapsto\sigma(n) - 1$ are needed before a prime is reached?

Erdos409.erdos_409.variants.sigma_termin.docHtml: If $n > 1$ then the iteration $n\mapsto\sigma(n) - 1$ necessarily reaches a prime. Note: this is open — it is not clear that the σ iteration always terminates, since it is non-decreasing (unlike the φ iteration which is strictly decreasing).

Erdos409.erdos_409.variants.sigma_isThet.docHtml: Let $c(n)$ be the minimum number of iterations of $n\mapsto\sigma(n) - 1$ before a prime is reached. What is $\Theta(c(n))$?

Erdos409.erdos_409.variants.sigma_isBigO.docHtml: Let $c(n)$ be the minimum number of iterations of $n\mapsto\sigma(n) - 1$ before a prime is reached. Find the simplest function $g(n)$ such that $c(n) = O(g(n))$?

Erdos409.erdos_409.variants.sigma_isLitt.docHtml: Let $c(n)$ be the minimum number of iterations of $n\mapsto\sigma(n) - 1$ before a prime is reached. Find the simplest function $g(n)$ such that $c(n) = o(g(n))$?

Erdos409.erdos_409.variants.sigma_prime_.docHtml: Is it true that iterates of $n\mapsto\sigma(n) - 1$ always reach a prime?

Erdos497.erdos_497.docHtml:
How many antichains in $[n]$ are there? That is, how many families of subsets of $[n]$ are there such that, if $\mathcal{F}$ is such a family and $A,B\in \mathcal{F}$, then $A\not\subseteq B$?

Sperner's theorem states that $\lvert \mathcal{F}\rvert \leq \binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$. This is also known as Dedekind's problem. Resolved by Kleitman [Kl69], who proved that the number of such families is $$2^{(1+o(1))\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}}.$$

Erdos1092.f.docHtml:
Let $f_r(m)$ be maximal such that, if any graph $G$ has the property that every subgraph $H$ on $m$ vertices is the union of a graph with chromatic number $\leq r$ and a graph with $\leq f_r(m)$ edges, then $G$ has chromatic number $\leq r+1$.

The quantification is over all finite graphs $G$ (of any size), not just graphs on a fixed vertex set.

Erdos1092.f_asymptotic_2.docHtml:
Is it true that $f_2(n) \gg n$? Disproved by Rödl, who showed $f_r(n) = o(n)$ for all fixed $r \geq 2$. A conjecture of Erdős, Hajnal, and Szemerédi.

This seems to be closely related to, but distinct from, 744.

Tang notes in the comments that Rödl [Ro82] constructed, for any $\epsilon>0$ and $k$, a graph with chromatic number $\geq k$ such that every graph on $m$ vertices is bipartite after deleting at most $\epsilon m$ edges.

Erdos1092.f_asymptotic_general.docHtml: More generally, is $f_r(n)\gg_r n$? Disproved by Rödl, who showed $f_r(n) = o(n)$ for all fixed $r \geq 2$.

Erdos275.erdos_275.docHtml:
If a finite system of $r$ congruences ${ a_i\pmod{n_i} : 1\leq i\leq r}$ (the $n_i$ are not necessarily distinct) covers $2^r$ consecutive integers then it covers all integers.

This is best possible as the system $2^{i-1}\pmod{2^i}$ shows. This was proved independently by Selfridge and Crittenden and Vanden Eynden [CrVE70].

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.

Erdos1080.IsBipartition.docHtml: IsBipartition G X Y means that X and Y form a bipartition of the vertices of G.

Erdos1080.erdos_1080.docHtml:
Let $G$ be a bipartite graph on $n$ vertices such that one part has $\lfloor n^{2/3}\rfloor$ vertices. Is there a constant $c>0$ such that if $G$ has at least $cn$ edges then $G$ must contain a $C_6$?

The answer is no, as shown by De Caen and Székely [DeSz92], who in fact show a stronger result. Let $f(n,m)$ be the maximum number of edges of a bipartite graph between $n$ and $m$ vertices which does not contain either a $C_4$ or $C_6$. A positive answer to this question would then imply $f(n,\lfloor n^{2/3}\rfloor)\ll n$. De Caen and Székely prove $n^{10/9}\gg f(n,\lfloor n^{2/3}\rfloor) \gg n^{58/57+o(1)}$ for $m\sim n^{2/3}$. They also prove more generally that, for $n^{1/2}\leq m\leq n$, $f(n,m) \ll (nm)^{2/3},$ which was also proved by Faudree and Simonovits.

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.

Erdos342.UniqueUlamSum.docHtml: UniqueUlamSum a n m means that $m$ has a unique representation as $a(i) + a(j)$ with $i < j < n$.

Erdos342.IsUlamSequence.docHtml: IsUlamSequence a means that $a$ is the Ulam sequence (OEIS A002858): $a(0) = 1$, $a(1) = 2$, and for each $n \geq 2$, $a(n)$ is the least integer greater than $a(n-1)$ that has a unique representation as $a(i) + a(j)$ with $i < j < n$.

Erdos342.erdos_342.test.a2.docHtml: $a(2) = 3$: the only pair $(i,j)$ with $i < j < 2$ is $(0,1)$, giving $1 + 2 = 3$.

Erdos342.erdos_342.test.a3.docHtml: $a(3) = 4$: among sums $> 3$ with a unique representation from ${1,2,3}$, the smallest is $4 = 1 + 3$. The candidate $5 = 2 + 3$ is ruled out by minimality since $4$ has a unique representation.

Erdos342.erdos_342.parts.i.docHtml: Do infinitely many pairs $(a, a+2)$ occur in Ulam's sequence?

Erdos342.erdos_342.parts.ii.docHtml: Does Ulam's sequence eventually have periodic differences? That is, is $a(n+1) - a(n)$ eventually periodic?

Erdos342.erdos_342.parts.iii.docHtml: Part (iii), is the density of the sequence 0?

Erdos1038.erdos_1038.parts.i.docHtml: What is the infimum of |{x ∈ ℝ : |f x| < 1}| over all nonconstant monic polynomials f such that all of its roots are real and contained in [-1,1]?

Erdos1038.erdos_1038.parts.ii.docHtml: The supremum of |{x ∈ ℝ : |f x| < 1}| over all monic polynomials f such that all of its roots are real and contained in [-1,1] is 2 * 2 ^ (1 / 2). This is proved in [Tao25].

Erdos1038.erdos_1038.variants.inf_upperB.docHtml: The infimum of |{x ∈ ℝ : |f x| < 1}| over all nonconstant monic polynomials f such that all of its roots are real and contained in [-1,1] is < 1.835.

Erdos1038.erdos_1038.varaints.inf_lowerB.docHtml: The infimum of |{x ∈ ℝ : |f x| < 1}| over all nonconstant monic polynomials f such that all of its roots are real and contained in [-1,1] is ≥ 2 ^ (4 / 3) - 1.

Erdos1074.EHSNumbers.docHtml: The EHS numbers (after Erdős, Hardy, and Subbarao) are those $m\geq 1$ such that there exists a prime $p\not\equiv 1\pmod{m}$ such that $m! + 1 \equiv 0\pmod{p}$.

Erdos1074.PillaiPrimes.docHtml: The Pillai primes are those primes $p$ such that there exists an $m \ge 1$ with $p\not\equiv 1\pmod{m}$ such that $m! + 1 \equiv 0\pmod{p}$

Erdos1074.erdos_1074.parts.i.docHtml: Let $S$ be the set of all $m\geq 1$ such that there exists a prime $p\not\equiv 1\pmod{m}$ such that $m! + 1 \equiv 0\pmod{p}$. Does $$ \lim\frac{|S\cap[1, x]|}{x} $$ exist?

Erdos1074.erdos_1074.parts.ii.docHtml: Let $S$ be the set of all $m\geq 1$ such that there exists a prime $p\not\equiv 1\pmod{m}$ such that $m! + 1 \equiv 0\pmod{p}$. What is $$ \lim\frac{|S\cap[1, x]|}{x}? $$

Erdos1074.erdos_1074.parts.iii.docHtml: Similarly, if $P$ is the set of all primes $p$ such that there exists an $m$ with $p\not\equiv 1\pmod{m}$ such that $m! + 1 \equiv 0\pmod{p}$, then does $$ \lim\frac{|P\cap[1, x]|}{\pi(x)} $$ exist?

Erdos1074.erdos_1074.parts.iv.docHtml: Similarly, if $P$ is the set of all primes $p$ such that there exists an $m$ with $p\not\equiv 1\pmod{m}$ such that $m! + 1 \equiv 0\pmod{p}$, then what is $$ \lim\frac{|P\cap[1, x]|}{\pi(x)}? $$

Erdos1074.erdos_1074.variants.mem_pillai.docHtml: Pillai [Pi30] raised the question of whether there exist any primes in $P$. This was answered by Chowla, who noted that, for example, $14! + 1 \equiv 18! + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{23}$.

Erdos1074.erdos_1074.variants.EHSNumbers.docHtml:
Erdős, Hardy, and Subbarao proved that $S$ is infinite.

Formal proof linked here provided by AlphaProof.

Erdos1074.erdos_1074.variants.PillaiPrim.docHtml: Erdős, Hardy, and Subbarao proved that $P$ is infinite.

Erdos1074.erdos_1074.variants.EHSNumbers.docHtml: Regarding the first question, Hardy and Subbarao computed all EHS numbers up to $2^{10}$, and write "...if this trend conditions we expect [the limit] to be around 0.5, if it exists."

Erdos180.FiniteGraph.docHtml: A finite graph, bundled with its vertex count, so that a family may mix orders.

Erdos180.FiniteGraph.order.docHtml: A finite graph, bundled with its vertex count, so that a family may mix orders.

Erdos180.FiniteGraph.graph.docHtml: A finite graph, bundled with its vertex count, so that a family may mix orders.

Erdos180.FamilyFree.docHtml: A host graph is family-free when it contains no member of family as a subgraph.

Erdos180.familyExtremal.docHtml: $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})$, the greatest number of edges of a graph on n vertices containing no member of family.

Erdos180.IsCyclicFamily.docHtml: No member of the family is acyclic.

Erdos180.IsCompactFamily.docHtml: The family is compact: some single member already controls the family extremal number.

Erdos180.erdos_180.docHtml:
If $\mathcal{F}$ is a finite set of finite graphs then $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})$ is the maximum number of edges a graph on $n$ vertices can have without containing any subgraphs from $\mathcal{F}$. Note that it is trivial that $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})\leq \mathrm{ex}(n;G)$ for every $G\in\mathcal{F}$. Is it true that, for every $\mathcal{F}$, there exists $G\in\mathcal{F}$ such that $$\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\ll_{\mathcal{F}}\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})?$$

This is the Erdős–Simonovits compactness conjecture. The answer is no: OpenAI [OpenAI26] give a family of connected bipartite graphs, none of them acyclic, for which no single member controls the family extremal number. See erdos_180.variants.counterexample.

Erdos180.erdos_180.variants.counterexamp.docHtml: The counterexample: a nonempty family of connected bipartite graphs, none acyclic, that is not compact.

Erdos757.IsAdmissible.docHtml: We say that c is admissible if for any finit set A such that for any subset B of size 4, (B - B).card = 11, there exists a Sidon subset S of size at least c * A.ncard.

Erdos757.erdos_757.docHtml: What is the supremum of the set of admissible numbers?

Erdos757.erdos_757.variants.lowerBound.docHtml: The supremum is strictly larger than 1 / 2, which is proved in [GyLe95].

Erdos757.erdos_757.variants.upperBound.docHtml: In [GyLe95], the authors also prove that the supremum is smaller than 3 / 5.

Erdos302.NoUnitFractionTriple.docHtml: A finite set $A$ of positive integers admits no solution to $\frac{1}{a} = \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c}$ with $a, b, c$ distinct elements of $A$.

Erdos302.IsMaxNoTripleCard.docHtml: $f N$ is the size of the largest $A ⊆ {1, …, N}$ containing no solution to $\frac{1}{a} = \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c}$ with distinct $a, b, c ∈ A$.

Erdos302.erdos_302.parts.i.docHtml:
Let $f(N)$ be the size of the largest $A\subseteq {1,\ldots,N}$ such that there are no solutions to $$\frac{1}{a}= \frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}$$ with distinct $a,b,c\in A$? Estimate $f(N)$.

The colouring version of this is [303], which was solved by Brown and Rödl [BrRo91].

Erdos302.erdos_302.parts.ii.docHtml:
In particular, is $f(N)=(\tfrac{1}{2}+o(1))N$?

This is false: it is contradicted by Cambie's lower bound of $(5/8+o(1))N$ recorded below, since $5/8 > 1/2$.

Erdos302.erdos_302.variants.lower_half.docHtml: One can take either $A$ to be all odd integers in $[1,N]$ or all integers in $[N/2,N]$ to show $f(N)\geq (1/2+o(1))N$.

Erdos302.erdos_302.variants.lower_five_e.docHtml: Stijn Cambie has observed that $$f(N)\geq (5/8+o(1))N,$$ taking $A$ to be all odd integers $\leq N/4$ and all integers in $[N/2,N]$.

Erdos302.erdos_302.variants.upper_nine_t.docHtml: Wouter van Doorn has proved [va25] that $$f(N) \leq (9/10+o(1))N.$$

Erdos291.L.docHtml: $L_n$ is the least common multiple of ${1,\ldots,n}$.

Erdos291.erdos_291.parts.i.docHtml:
Let $n\geq 1$ and define $L_n$ to be the least common multiple of ${1,\ldots,n}$ and $a_n$ by $\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\frac{1}{k}=\frac{a_n}{L_n}$.

Is it true that $(a_n,L_n)=1$ occurs for infinitely many $n$?

Erdos291.erdos_291.parts.ii.docHtml:
Is it true that $(a_n,L_n)>1$ occurs for infinitely many $n$?

Steinerberger has observed that the answer to the second question is trivially yes: for example, any $n$ which begins with a $2$ in base $3$ has $3\mid (a_n,L_n)$.

Erdos291.erdos_291.variants.steinerberge.docHtml: More generally, if the leading digit of $n$ in base $p$ is $p-1$ then $p\mid (a_n,L_n)$. There is in fact a necessary and sufficient condition: a prime $p\leq n$ divides $(a_n,L_n)$ if and only if $p$ divides the numerator of $1+\cdots+\frac{1}{k}$, where $k$ is the leading digit of $n$ in base $p$. This can be seen by writing $a_n = \frac{L_n}{1}+\cdots+\frac{L_n}{n}$ and observing that the right-hand side is congruent to $1+\cdots+1/k$ modulo $p$. (The previous claim about $p-1$ follows immediately from Wolstenholme's theorem.)

Erdos291.erdos_291.variants.shiu_heurist.docHtml: This leads to a heuristic prediction (see for example a preprint of Shiu [Sh16]) of $\asymp\frac{x}{\log x}$ for the number of $n\in [1,x]$ such that $(a_n,L_n)=1$.
In particular, there should be infinitely many $n$, but the set of such $n$ should have density zero. Unfortunately this heuristic is difficult to turn into a proof.

Erdos291.erdos_291.variants.wu_yan.docHtml: Wu and Yan [WuYa22] have proved, conditional on $\frac{1}{\log p}$ being linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ for any finite collection of primes $p$ (itself a consequence of Schanuel's conjecture), that the set of $n$ for which $(a_n,L_n)>1$ has upper density $1$.

Erdos195.erdos_195.docHtml: What is the largest $k$ such that in any permutation of $\mathbb{Z}$ there must exist a monotone $k$-term arithmetic progression $x_1 < \cdots < x_k$?

Erdos918.erdos_918.parts.i.docHtml: Is there a graph with $\aleph_2$ vertices and chromatic number $\aleph_2$ such that every subgraph on $\aleph_1$ vertices has chromatic number $\leq\aleph_0$?

Erdos918.erdos_918.parts.ii.docHtml: Is there a graph with $\aleph_{\omega+1}$ vertices and chromatic number $\aleph_1$ such that every subgraph on $\aleph_\omega$ vertices has chromatic number $\leq\aleph_0$?

Erdos918.erdos_918.variants.all_subgraph.docHtml: Is there a graph with $\aleph_2$ vertices and chromatic number $\aleph_2$ such that every subgraph on $\aleph_1$ vertices has chromatic number $\leq\aleph_0$?
Is there a graph with $\aleph_{\omega+1}$ vertices and chromatic number $\aleph_1$ such that every subgraph on $\aleph_\omega$ vertices has chromatic number $\leq\aleph_0$?

Erdos918.erdos_918.variants.erdos_hajnal.docHtml: A question of Erd\H{o}s and Hajnal [ErHa68b], who proved that for every finite $k$ there is a graph with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ and $\aleph_k$ vertices where each subgraph on less than $\aleph_k$ vertices has chromatic number $\leq \aleph_0$.

Erdos918.erdos_918.variants.eq_aleph_0.p.docHtml:
In [ErHa69] the questions are stated with $= \aleph_0$ rather than $\leq\aleph_0$. This is a likely typo since it can be shown that no such graph exists in this case.

This is the first question with induced subgraphs.

Erdos918.erdos_918.variants.eq_aleph_0_a.docHtml:
In [ErHa69] the questions are stated with $= \aleph_0$ rather than $\leq\aleph_0$. This is a likely typo since it can be shown that no such graph exists in this case.

This is the first question with all subgraphs.

Erdos918.erdos_918.variants.eq_aleph_0.p.docHtml:
In [ErHa69] the questions are stated with $= \aleph_0$ rather than $\leq\aleph_0$. This is a likely typo since it can be shown that no such graph exists in this case.

This is the second question with induced subgraphs.

Erdos918.erdos_918.variants.eq_aleph_0_a.docHtml:
In [ErHa69] the questions are stated with $= \aleph_0$ rather than $\leq\aleph_0$. This is a likely typo since it can be shown that no such graph exists in this case.

This is the second question with all subgraphs.

Erdos43.f.docHtml: Let $f(N)$ be the maximum possible size of a Sidon set in ${1,\ldots,N}$.

Erdos43.erdos_43.parts.i.docHtml:
If $A$ and $B$ are Sidon sets in ${1,\ldots,N}$ with $(A-A)\cap(B-B)={0}$, is it true that $$\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}\leq\binom{f(N)}{2}+O(1)?$$

The answer is no; the Erdős Problems page notes that this follows from the solution to Erdős Problem 42.

Erdos43.erdos_43.parts.ii.docHtml:
If $A$ and $B$ are equal-sized Sidon sets in ${1,\ldots,N}$ with $(A-A)\cap(B-B)={0}$, can the bound be improved to $$\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2} \leq (1-c+o(1))\binom{f(N)}{2}$$ for some constant $c>0$?

The answer is no; the Erdős Problems page records a negative answer due to Barreto.

Erdos562.erdos_562.docHtml:
Let $R_r(n)$ denote the $r$-uniform hypergraph Ramsey number: the minimal $m$ such that if we $2$-colour all edges of the complete $r$-uniform hypergraph on $m$ vertices then there must be some monochromatic copy of the complete $r$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices.

Prove that, for $r \ge 3$, $$ \log_{r-1} R_r(n) \asymp_r n, $$ where $\log_{r-1}$ denotes the $(r-1)$-fold iterated logarithm.

Erdos199.erdos_199.docHtml:
If $A\subset \mathbb{R}$ does not contain a 3-term arithmetic progression then must $\mathbb{R}\backslash A$ contain an infinite arithmetic progression?

Baumgartner [Ba75] answered this in the negative.

Erdos659.erdos_659.docHtml:
Is there a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that every subset of $4$ points determines at least $3$ distances, yet the total number of distinct distances is $\ll \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}$?

There does exist such a set: a suitable truncation of the lattice ${(a,b\sqrt{2}): a,b\in\mathbb{Z}}$ suffices. This construction appears to have been first considered by Moree and Osburn \cite{MoOs06}, who proved that it has $\ll \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}$ many distinct distances. This construction was independently found by Lund and Sheffer, who further noted that this configuration contains no squares or equilateral triangles.

There are only six possible configurations of $4$ points which determine only $2$ distances (first noted by Erdős and Fishburn [ErFi96]), and five of them contain either a square or an equilateral triangle. The remaining configuration contains four points from a regular pentagon, and Grayzel [Gr26] (using Gemini) has noted in the comments that this configuration can also be ruled out, thus giving a complete solution to this problem.

Boris Alexeev provides a formalisation of the reduction, which is conditional on Bernays' theorem (assumed as an axiom in the proof to obtain the $O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$ bound). See the formal proof.

Erdos206.egyptianSum.docHtml: The Egyptian fraction sum: ∑_{m ∈ S} 1/m for a finset of natural numbers.

Erdos206.IsUnderapprox.docHtml: S is an Egyptian underapproximation of x: valid denominators (all positive) and sum < x.

Erdos206.IsBestNTerm.docHtml: S achieves the best n-term Egyptian underapproximation of x, i.e. egyptianSum S realises $R_n(x)$.

Erdos206.EventuallyGreedy.docHtml: x has eventually greedy best Egyptian underapproximations: from some n₀ on, the best n-term underapproximations of x are the prefixes of a single strictly increasing sequence of denominators, so each is obtained from the previous by appending the minimal admissible denominator.

Erdos206.erdos_206.docHtml:
Let $x>0$ be a real number. For any $n\geq 1$ let $$R_n(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{m_i}<x$$ be the maximal sum of $n$ distinct unit fractions which is $<x$.

Is it true that, for almost all $x$, for sufficiently large $n$, we have $$R_{n+1}(x)=R_n(x)+\frac{1}{m},$$ where $m$ is minimal such that $m$ does not appear in $R_n(x)$ and the right-hand side is $<x$? (That is, are the best underapproximations eventually always constructed in a 'greedy' fashion?)

Kovač [Ko24b] has proved that this is false - in fact as false as possible: the set of $x\in (0,\infty)$ for which the best underapproximations are eventually 'greedy' has Lebesgue measure zero.

Erdos1193.erdos_1193.parts.i.docHtml:
Let $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ and let $g(n)$ be a non-decreasing function of $n$ which is always $>0$.

Is the lower density of $${ n : 1_A\ast 1_A(n)=g(n)}$$ always $0$?

The answer is trivially no to both questions: indeed if $A=\mathbb{N}$ (assuming $0\in\mathbb{N}$) then $1_A\ast 1_A(n)=n+1$ for all $n$. Presumably Erdős had some additional restrictions on either $g$ or $A$ in mind, but these are not recorded in [Er80].

Erdos1193.erdos_1193.parts.ii.docHtml:
Let $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ and let $g(n)$ be a non-decreasing function of $n$ which is always $>0$.

Is the upper density of $${ n : 1_A\ast 1_A(n)=g(n)}$$ always $<c$ for some constant $c<1$?

The answer is trivially no to both questions: indeed if $A=\mathbb{N}$ (assuming $0\in\mathbb{N}$) then $1_A\ast 1_A(n)=n+1$ for all $n$. Presumably Erdős had some additional restrictions on either $g$ or $A$ in mind, but these are not recorded in [Er80].

Erdos1193.erdos_1193.variants.upper_dens.docHtml: Erdős writes the upper density can be positive, but he believes it is bounded away from $1$.

Erdos46.erdos_46.docHtml:
Does every finite colouring of the integers have a monochromatic solution to $1=\sum \frac{1}{n_i}$ with $2\leq n_1<\cdots <n_k$?

The answer is yes, as proved by Croot [Cr03] - indeed, there are infinitely many disjoint such monochromatic solutions.

Erdos46.erdos_46.variants.infinitely_man.docHtml: Croot [Cr03] proved more: there are infinitely many disjoint such monochromatic solutions.

Erdos46.erdos_46.variants.positive_rat.docHtml: In [ErGr80] they also ask for a monochromatic representation of any $\frac{a}{b}>0$.

Erdos456.m.docHtml: Let $m_n$ be the smallest integer such that $n\mid \phi(m_n)$.

Erdos456.erdos_456.parts.i.docHtml: Is it true that $m_n<p_n$ for almost all $n$?

Erdos456.erdos_456.parts.iii.docHtml: Are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p-1$ is the only $n$ for which $m_n=p$?

Erdos456.erdos_456.variants.mn_leq_pn.docHtml: It is trivial that $m_n \leq p_n$ always.

Erdos456.erdos_456.variants.infinitely_m.docHtml: Erdős [Er79e] writes it is 'easy to show' that for infinitely many $n$ we have $m_n < p_n$.

Erdos456.erdos_456.variants.m_div_n.docHtml: Erdős [Er79e] writes it is 'easy to show' that $m_n/n \to \infty$ for almost all $n$.

Erdos519.powerSum.docHtml: The $k$th power sum of a finite sequence of complex numbers.

Erdos519.erdos_519.docHtml:
Let $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in \mathbb{C}$ with $z_1=1$. Must there exist an absolute constant $c>0$ such that $$ \max_{1\leq k\leq n}\left\lvert \sum_{i}z_i^k\right\rvert>c? $$

Atkinson proved that $c=1/6$ suffices.

Erdos349.IsGoodPair.docHtml: This defines the core property of the problem: For what values of $t,\alpha \in (0,\infty)$ is the sequence $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ complete?

Erdos349.erdos_349.docHtml: For what values of $t,\alpha \in (0,\infty)$ is the sequence $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ complete (that is, all sufficiently large integers are the sum of distinct integers of the form $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$)?

Erdos349.complete_for_alpha_in_Ioo_one_t.docHtml: It seems likely that the sequence is complete for all for all $t>0$ and all $1 < \alpha < \frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$.

Erdos349.exists_t_for_k_disjoint_segment.docHtml: For any $k$ there exists some $t_k\in (0,1)$ such that the set of $\alpha$ such that the sequence $\lfloor t_k\alpha^n\rfloor$ is complete consists of at least $k$ disjoint line segments.

Erdos349.erdos_349.variants.floor_3_halv.docHtml: Is it true that the terms of the sequence $\lfloor (3/2)^n\rfloor$ are odd infinitely often and even infinitely often?
Is it true that the terms of the sequence $\lfloor (3/2)^n\rfloor$ are even infinitely often?

Erdos349.alpha_gt_two_not_isGoodPair.docHtml:
For $\alpha > 2$ and any $t > 0$, the sequence $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ is not additively complete; equivalently $(t, \alpha)$ is not a "good pair". A partial result on the open Erdős Problem 349: it complements complete_for_alpha_in_Ioo_one_to_goldenRatio.

The proof is recorded via the formal_proof mechanism rather than written inline, as it exceeds the repository's proof-length guideline.

Erdos349.alpha_le_one_not_isGoodPair.docHtml: For $0 < \alpha \le 1$ and any $t > 0$, $(t, \alpha)$ is not a good pair: every term $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ lies in the finite interval $[0, \lfloor t\rfloor]$ (since $\alpha^n \le 1$), so every subset sum is bounded by the constant $\sum_{i \in [0,\lfloor t\rfloor]} i$, and no large integer can be a subset sum. A partial result on the open Erdős Problem 349, complementing the $2 < \alpha$ and integer-coefficient cases.

Erdos349.exists_finset_sum_two_pow.docHtml: Binary expansion. Every natural number $k$ is a sum of distinct powers of two: there is a finite set $E$ of exponents with $k = \sum_{i \in E} 2^i$. Proved by strong induction: subtract the largest power $2^m \le k$, recurse on the remainder.

Erdos349.one_two_isGoodPair.docHtml: The pair $(1, 2)$ is good. The powers of two $\lfloor 1\cdot 2^n\rfloor = 2^n$ form an additively complete set: every $k \ge 1$ is a finite sum of distinct powers of two.

Erdos349.dyadic_two_isGoodPair.docHtml: The dyadic fiber at $\alpha = 2$. For every $k$, the pair $(1/2^k, 2)$ is good: the sequence $\lfloor 2^n / 2^k\rfloor$ is additively complete because at index $n = m + k$ it equals the exact power $2^m$, so its range contains all powers of two, which already form an additively complete set. Uses monotonicity IsAddComplete.mono.

Erdos349.int_coeff_ge_two_not_isGoodPair.docHtml: Integer leading coefficient $t \ge 2$ blocks completeness. For every integer base $\alpha$, the pair $(t, \alpha)$ with integer $t \ge 2$ is not good: $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor = t\alpha^n$ is a multiple of $t$, so every subset sum is too, but two consecutive large integers cannot both be multiples of $t$. Generalizes the parity obstruction ($t = 2$). A partial result on Erdős Problem 349.

Erdos349.integer_isGoodPair_iff.docHtml: Erdős Problem 349, complete characterization on positive integer pairs. For integers $t \ge 1$, $\alpha \ge 1$, the pair $(t, \alpha)$ is good (i.e. $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ is additively complete) iff $(t, \alpha) = (1, 2)$. Assembles the four partial results: $(1,2)$ is good, $\alpha \le 1$ fails, $2 < \alpha$ fails (alpha_gt_two_not_isGoodPair), and integer $t \ge 2$ fails.

Erdos92.maxEquidistantPointsAt.docHtml: For a given point x and a set of other points, this function finds the maximum number of points that lie on a single circle centered at x. It does this by grouping the other points by their distance to x and finding the size of the largest group.

Erdos92.hasMinEquidistantProperty.docHtml: This property holds for a set of points A if every point x in A has at least k other points from A that are equidistant from x.

Erdos92.possible_f_values.docHtml: The set of all possible values k for which there exists a set of n points satisfying the hasMinEquidistantProperty k. The function f(n) will be the supremum of this set.

Erdos92.possible_f_values_BddAbove.docHtml: A sanity check to ensure the set of possible f(n) values is bounded above. A trivial bound is n, since the points equidistant from any x form a subset of the other n - 1 points. This ensures sSup is well-defined.

Erdos92.f.docHtml: Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that there exists a set $A$ of $n$ points in $\mathbb^2$ in which every $x \in A$ has at least $f(n)$ points in $A$ equidistant from $x$.

Erdos92.erdos_92.variants.strong.docHtml: Or even $f(n) < n^{c/\log\log n}$ for some constant $c > 0$?

Erdos1043.erdos_1043.docHtml:
Erdős Problem 1043: Let $f\in \mathbb{C}[x]$ be a monic polynomial. Must there exist a straight line $\ell$ such that the projection of $${ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert\leq 1}$$ onto $\ell$ has measure at most $2$?

Pommerenke [Po61] proved that the answer is no.

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.

Erdos1043.erdos_1043.variants.weak.docHtml: On the other hand, Pommerenke also proved there always exists a line such that the projection has measure at most 3.3.

Erdos326.erdos_326.docHtml:
Let $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ be an additive basis of order 2.

Must there exist $B = {b_1 < b_2 < \dots} \subseteq A$ which is also a basis such that $\lim_{k\to\infty} \frac{b_k}{k^2}$ does not exist?

Erdos326.erdos_326.variants.eq.docHtml: Erdős originally asked whether this was true with A = B, but this was disproved by Cassels.

Erdos1060.erdos_1060.parts.i.docHtml: The conjecture is about the function $f(n)$ which counts the number of solutions to $k\sigma(k)=n$, where $\sigma(k)$ is the sum of divisors of $k$. The first bound is that $f(n)$ grows slower than any power of $n^(\frac{1}{\log\log n})$. The second bound is that $f(n)$ is at most a power of $\log n$.

Erdos1060.erdos_1060.parts.ii.docHtml: Part (ii) of Erdős Problem 1060: bound on the number of $k \le n$ with $k \sigma_1(k) = n$.

Erdos537.erdos_537.docHtml:
Let $\epsilon>0$ and $N$ be sufficiently large. If $A\subseteq {1,\ldots,N}$ has $\lvert A\rvert \geq \epsilon N$ then must there exist $a_1,a_2,a_3\in A$ and distinct primes $p_1,p_2,p_3$ such that $$a_1p_1=a_2p_2=a_3p_3?$$

A positive answer would imply [536].

Erdős describes a construction of Ruzsa which disproves this: consider the set of all squarefree numbers of the shape $p_1\cdots p_r$ where $p_{i+1}>2p_i$ for $1\leq i<r$. This set has positive density, and hence if $A$ is its intersection with $(N/2,N)$ then $\lvert A\rvert \gg N$ for all large $N$. Suppose now that $p_1a_1=p_2a_2=p_3a_3$ where $a_i\in A$ and $p_1,p_2,p_3$ are distinct primes. Without loss of generality we may assume that $a_2>a_3$ and hence $p_2<p_3$, and so since $p_2p_3\mid a_1\in A$ we must have $2<p_3/p_2$. On the other hand $p_3/p_2=a_2/a_3\in (1,2)$, a contradiction.

Erdos587.MaxNotSqSum.docHtml: MaxNotSqSum N is the size of the largest subset A of {1,...,N} such that for all non-empty S ⊆ A, the sum ∑ n ∈ S, n is not a square.

Erdos587.erdos_587.variants.nguyen_vu.docHtml: Nguyen and Vu proved that $|A| \ll N^{1/3} (\log N)^{O(1)}$.

Erdos566.erdos_566.docHtml:
Let $G$ be such that any subgraph on $k$ vertices has at most $2k-3$ edges. Is it true that, if $H$ has $m$ edges and no isolated vertices, then $\hat{r}(G,H) \ll m$?

In other words: if $G$ is sparse (every induced subgraph on $k$ vertices has $≤ 2k-3$ edges), is $G$ Ramsey size linear?

Erdos680.erdos_680.parts.i.docHtml: Is it true that, for all sufficiently large $n$, there exists some $k$ such that $$ p(n+k)>k^2+1, $$ where $p(m)$ denotes the least prime factor of $m$?

Erdos680.erdos_680.parts.ii.docHtml: Can one prove this is false if we replace $k^2+1$ by $e^{(1+\epsilon)\sqrt{k}}+C_\epsilon$, for all $\epsilon>0$, where $C_\epsilon>0$ is some constant?

Erdos346.erdos_346.docHtml: Is it true that for every lacunary, strongly complete sequence A that is not complete whenever infinitely many terms are removed from it, lim A (n + 1) / A n = (1 + √5) / 2?

Erdos346.f.docHtml: We define a sequence f by the formula f n = n.fib - (- 1) ^ n.

Erdos346.erdos_346.variants.f_isAddStron.docHtml: The sequence f is strongly complete, and this is proved in [Gr64d].

Erdos346.erdos_346.variants.f_not_isAddC.docHtml: The sequence f is not complete whenever infinitely many terms are removed from it, and this is proved in [Gr64d].

Erdos346.erdos_346.variants.gt_goldenRat.docHtml: Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] remark that it is easy to see that if A (n + 1) / A n > (1 + √5) / 2 then the second property is automatically satisfied.

Erdos346.erdos_346.variants.example.docHtml: Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] also say that it is not hard to construct very irregular sequences satisfying the aforementioned properties.

Erdos160.erdos_160.h.docHtml: Let $h(n)$ be the smallest $k$ such that ${1,\ldots,n}$ can be coloured with $k$ colours so that every four-term arithmetic progression must contain at least three distinct colours.

Erdos160.erdos_160.known_upper.docHtml: On Mathoverflow user leechlattice shows that $h(n) \ll n^{\frac 2 3}$.

Erdos160.erdos_160.better_upper.docHtml: Estimate $h(n)$ by finding a better upper bound.

Erdos160.erdos_160.better_lower.docHtml: Estimate $h(n)$ by finding a better lower bound.

Erdos160.erdos_160.variants.known_lower.docHtml: The observation of Zachary Hunter in that question coupled with the bounds of Kelley-Meka KeMe23 imply that $$h(N) \gg \exp(c(\log N)^{\frac 1 {12}})$$ for some $c > 0$.

Erdos289.erdos_289.docHtml: Is it true that, for all sufficiently large $k$, there exists finite intervals $I_1, \dotsc, I_k \subset \mathbb{N}$ with $|I_i| \geq 2$ for $1 \leq i \leq k$ such that $$ 1 = \sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{n \in I_i} \frac{1}{n}. $$

Erdos1051.GrowthCondition.docHtml: A sequence of integers a satisfies the growth condition if $\liminf a_n^{\frac{1}{2^n}} > 1$.

Erdos1051.erdos_1051.docHtml:
Is it true that if $a_0 < a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ is a strictly increasing sequence of integers with $\liminf a_n^{1/2^n} > 1$, then the series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{1}{a_n \cdot a_{n+1}}$ is irrational?

This was solved in the affirmative by Aletheia [Fe26]. This was extended by Barreto, Kang, Kim, Kovač, and Zhang [BKKKZ26], who essentially give a complete answer: if $\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$ is the golden ratio and $1\leq a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ is a monotonically increasing sequence of integers such that $\limsup a_n^{1/\phi^{n}}=\infty$ then $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{a_na_{n+1}}$ is irrational. Conversely, for any $1 < C < \infty$ there exists a sequence of integers $1\leq a_1<\cdots$ such that $\lim a_n^{1/\phi^{n}}=C$ where this infinite sum is a rational number.

(Further, more general, results are available in [BKKKZ26].)

This was formalized in Lean by Baretto.

Erdos1051.erdos_1051.variants.rapid_grow.docHtml: Erdős [Er88c] notes that if the sequence grows rapidly to infinity (specifically, if $a_{n+1} \geq C \cdot a_n^2$ for some constant $C > 0$), then the series is irrational.

Erdos639.erdos_639.docHtml:
Is it true that if the edges of $K_n$ are 2-coloured then there are at most $n^2/4$ many edges which do not occur in a monochromatic triangle?

Solved by Erdős, Rousseau, and Schelp for large $n$, but unpublished. Alon has observed that this also follows from a result of Pyber [Py86], which states that (for large enough $n$) at most $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+2$ monochromatic cliques cover all edges of a $2$-coloured $K_n$.

This problem was solved completely by Keevash and Sudakov [KeSu04], who proved that the correct threshold is $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ for all $n\geq 7$, is $\binom{n}{2}$ for $n\leq 5$, and is $10$ for $n=6$.

Since the bound fails for small $n$ (at $n=6$ the threshold is $10 > 6^2/4$), the statement is formalized in the asymptotic reading in which the problem was posed and solved: for all sufficiently large $n$, every $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ leaves at most $n^2/4$ edges not occurring in a monochromatic triangle. Edges of $K_n$ are the non-diagonal unordered pairs Sym2 (Fin n); an edge ${x, y}$ occurs in a monochromatic triangle if and only if there is a third vertex $z$ with $C({x, z}) = C({y, z}) = C({x, y})$.

The linked file proves the bound for every finite vertex type with at least $10$ vertices, which gives the atTop reading below, and collects the uncovered edges as the edge set of a graph rather than as a set of pairs.

Erdos66.erdos_66.docHtml: Is there and $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ is such that $$\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{1_A\ast 1_A(n)}{\log n}$$ exists and is $\ne 0$?

Erdos1022.SparseImpliesPropertyB.docHtml: SparseImpliesPropertyB t c asserts that every finite family F of finite sets, all of size at least t, such that for every nonempty finite set X there are < c * |X| many A ∈ F with A ⊆ X, has property B.

Erdos1022.erdos_1022.docHtml:
Is there a constant $c_t$, where $c_t\to \infty$ as $t\to \infty$, such that if $\mathcal{F}$ is a finite family of finite sets, all of size at least $t$, and for every set $X$ there are $<c_t\lvert X\rvert$ many $A\in \mathcal{F}$ with $A\subseteq X$, then $\mathcal{F}$ has chromatic number $2$ (in other words, has property B)?

This is false, and $c_t<2$ for all $t$: a counterexample is provided by Wood [Wo13b], who constructs, for any $r\geq 2$, a triangle-free $2$-degenerate $r$-uniform hypergraph with chromatic number $3$. A similar counterexample was found independently by KoishiChan in the comments.

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.

Erdos1022.erdos_1022.variants.lt_two.docHtml: This is false, and $c_t<2$ for all $t$: a counterexample is provided by Wood [Wo13b], who constructs, for any $r\geq 2$, a triangle-free $2$-degenerate $r$-uniform hypergraph with chromatic number $3$. A similar counterexample was found independently by KoishiChan in the comments.

Erdos1022.erdos_1022.variants.lovasz.docHtml: Erdős originally conjectured, in this language, that $c_2=1$, which he reports in [Er71] was proved by Lovász.

Erdos1084.f.docHtml: The maximal number of pairs of points which are distance 1 apart that a set of n 1-separated points in ℝ^d make.

Erdos1084.erdos_1084.variants.upper_d1.docHtml: It is easy to check that $f_1(n) = n - 1$.

Erdos1084.erdos_1084.variants.easy_upper.docHtml: It is easy to check that $f_2(n) < 3n$.

Erdos1084.erdos_1084.variants.upper_d2.docHtml: Erdős showed that there is some constant $c > 0$ such that $f_2(n) < 3n - c n^{1/2}$.

Erdos1084.erdos_1084.variants.triangular.docHtml:
Erdős conjectured that the triangular lattice is best possible in 2D, in particular that $f_2(3n^2 + 3n + 1) < 9n^2 + 3n$.

Note: in [Er75f] is read $9n^2 + 6n$, but this seems to be a typo.

Erdos1084.erdos_1084.variants.upper_lowe.docHtml: Erdős claims the existence of two constants $c_1, c_2 > 0$ such that $6n - c_1 n^{2/3} ≤ f_3(n) \le 6n - c_2 n^{2/3}$.

Erdos348.erdos_348.docHtml:
For what values of $0 \leq m < n$ is there a complete sequence $A = {a_1 \leq a_2 \leq \cdots}$ of integers such that

    $A$ remains complete after removing any $m$ elements, but

    $A$ is not complete after removing any $n$ elements.

Erdos701.erdos_701.docHtml: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of sets closed under taking subsets (i.e. if $B\subseteq A\in\mathcal{F}$ then $B\in \mathcal{F}$). There exists some element $x$ such that whenever $\mathcal{F}'\subseteq \mathcal{F}$ is an intersecting subfamily we have $$\lvert \mathcal{F}'\rvert \leq \lvert { A\in \mathcal{F} : x\in A}\rvert.$$

Erdos421.erdos_421.docHtml: Is there a sequence $1 \le d_1 < d_2 < \dots$ with density 1 such that all products $\prod_{u \le i \le v} d_i$ are distinct?

Erdos769.Cube.docHtml: An axis-parallel homothetic copy of the standard n-cube.

Erdos769.Cube.lower.docHtml: An axis-parallel homothetic copy of the standard n-cube.

Erdos769.Cube.side.docHtml: An axis-parallel homothetic copy of the standard n-cube.

Erdos769.Cube.Mem.docHtml: Membership in the half-open cube ∏ j, [lower j, lower j + side).

Erdos769.InUnit.docHtml: Membership in the half-open unit cube [0,1)^n.

Erdos769.Cube.InsideUnit.docHtml: A cube is nondegenerate and contained in the closed unit cube.

Erdos769.IsTiling.docHtml: tiles is an exact decomposition of the unit n-cube into k homothetic cubes: every tile is a positive homothet inside the unit cube, and every point of [0,1)^n belongs to exactly one half-open tile.
